design_detail: Narrative review with a reported literature search: PubMed, PsycINFO and ScienceDirect with printed search terms, plus reference lists and Google Scholar. Inclusion criteria, stated to have been formulated before the literature search: participants aged 16 or older; methamphetamine specifically (not amphetamine or other stimulants); studies of methamphetamine psychosis that directly compared it with schizophrenia or a primary psychotic disorder; methamphetamine use preceding the psychosis; original research only; no case studies. Search dates, numbers of records screened and excluded, language limits, duplicate screening and any risk-of-bias tool are not reported, and one author conducted the review (Author contributions). Twelve direct-comparison studies published 1990–2017 are tabulated in Table 1; Table 2 appraises thirteen informally (it adds Hajebi et al., 2018). No meta-analysis: narrative synthesis organized by positive, negative and cognitive symptoms and by acute versus chronic (persistent) methamphetamine psychosis.
can_establish: What the small set of direct comparisons published up to 2018 reported about positive, negative and cognitive symptoms in methamphetamine psychosis versus schizophrenia, and which methodological weaknesses those studies share.
cannot_establish: That the eligible literature was found completely (undated search, no record flow, single reviewer); the size or consistency of any group difference (no effect sizes, no pooling); or that any symptom reliably separates methamphetamine psychosis from schizophrenia, because several headline differences rest on indirect comparisons or single small studies. The prevalence, duration and transition figures in its introduction are second-hand citations outside the review's own method.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). The included studies recruited mostly from psychiatric hospitals, emergency wards, in- and outpatient clinics and detention centres in Taiwan, Iran, Japan, Norway, South Africa, Thailand and the USA, plus two Australian samples of people who use methamphetamine (needle and syringe programmes, Hides et al., 2015; a treatment cohort, McKetin et al., 2017) (Table 1). Per-study sizes as printed in Table 1 range from 22 to 285.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Human participants aged 16 or older; methamphetamine only; studies of methamphetamine psychosis directly compared with schizophrenia or primary psychotic disorder; methamphetamine use had to precede the psychosis; original research only (reviews excluded); case studies excluded (Overview of review › Inclusion criteria). The criteria list numbers two items as (3).
sample.demographics: Not summarized at review level. Table 1 gives sex and age for a few studies only: 61% men, mean age 31.65 (Hides et al., 2015); 71% men, mean age 31.6 (McKetin et al., 2017); 52% men, mean age about 38–39 (Medhus et al., 2013).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. The review does not report how many records were retrieved, screened or excluded.
sample.selection_effects: Review level: an undated search with no flow diagram and no list of excluded studies, run by one author, leaves completeness unverifiable. Study level: most psychosis samples were hospitalized, which the authors note selects more severe cases (Methodological limitations, 3rd paragraph); in two studies the primary-psychosis comparison group were themselves people who use methamphetamine (Hides et al., 2015; McKetin et al., 2017); in one, the schizophrenia group was chosen because it responded poorly to medication (Srisurapanont et al., 2011) (Table 2).

exposure.measurement: Not measured by the review. In the included studies methamphetamine-associated psychosis was established by structured interview (DIGS-C, SCID-I, CIDI, MINI-Plus), hospital files or chart review, and in one study by urine or blood toxicology (Medhus et al., 2013) (Tables 1–2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Barely reported: one psychosis group had used methamphetamine for a mean of 3.8 (SD 5.4) years (Srisurapanont et al., 2011); one recruited people who had injected moderate or high doses over an extended period (Tomiyama, 1990) (Table 1). No amounts, frequencies or routes are synthesized.
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled at review level. Table 2 records substantial other-drug use in psychosis groups: 66% with a history of other drug use (Ezzatpanah et al., 2014), 64% with other drug dependence (Tomiyama, 1990), 87% with at least one other psychoactive substance in blood or urine (Medhus et al., 2013). Shelly et al. (2016) excluded dependence on other drugs; most studies did not address it. The authors list uncontrolled polydrug use as a limitation (Methodological limitations, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Mostly not reported. The authors classified every study that did not report abstinence as an acute-psychosis study (Methodological limitations, 1st paragraph). Where reported: no more than 4 weeks (Shelly et al., 2016); methamphetamine use in the past week (Srisurapanont et al., 2011); more than 1 month (Wang et al., 2016); the acute group of Chen et al. (2015) was assessed about 9 weeks after its episode (Table 2).

comparison.controls: A schizophrenia or primary-psychosis group in every included study; healthy controls in only three (Chen et al., 2015; Ezzatpanah et al., 2014; Okada et al., 2016) (Table 2). The comparison group of Hajebi et al. (2018) mixed schizophrenia (46), schizoaffective disorder (1) and brief psychotic disorder (3), and 9 of its members had used methamphetamine (Table 2).
comparison.matching: Varies by study: age and sex matched in Ezzatpanah et al. (also education), Okada et al. and Tomiyama; groups differed in age, ethnicity and place of birth in Jacobs et al. (2008); age not matched in Srisurapanont et al. (2011) (Table 2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No included study had a pre-psychosis baseline. Premorbid ability was estimated only in some (Japanese Adult Reading Test in Okada and Yamamuro; WRAT reading in Jacobs). Family history and premorbid psychiatric risk are not compared between groups anywhere in the review.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Schizophrenia groups excluded substance use disorders in some studies (Chen 2015; Wang 2016; Shelly 2016), were methamphetamine users in others (Hides 2015; McKetin 2017), and had unknown drug use in Srisurapanont 2011 (Table 2).

outcomes.instruments: Across the included studies: BPRS, PANSS (including a five-factor model), SANS, Manchester Scale, SCID-I first-rank symptom items, CIDI lifetime symptom items; cognition with BACS, WCST, Stroop, Visual Search and Attention Test (VSAT), Wechsler Memory Scale, RBANS, WASI, D-KEFS colour-word interference, a continuous performance test, Trail Making and Grooved Pegboard; prefrontal activation with near-infrared spectroscopy (Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: Instrument validity in methamphetamine samples is not discussed, except the authors' argument that total-score scales such as PANSS and BPRS cannot capture qualitative differences in hallucinations and delusions (Methodological limitations, 3rd paragraph). Cognitive findings are group comparisons; none is related to norms.
outcomes.operationalization: Acute versus persistent methamphetamine psychosis is defined by whether psychosis continued for more than 1 month after stopping use, following Chen et al. (2015) (Methodological limitations, 1st paragraph); studies with unknown abstinence were counted as acute. Differences are reported only as significant or not.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not addressed by the review. Several included studies compared many single symptoms or tests (first-rank symptom items, lifetime symptom items, item-level differential item functioning) with no correction mentioned.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported for any included study.

analysis.effect_sizes: None reported by the review, which gives directions and significance only. Editors' calculation for Shelly et al. (2016), from the review's percentages and the Table 1 group sizes (methamphetamine psychosis n=33, schizophrenia n=69; counts reconstructed by rounding): voices conversing 16/33 vs 14/69, odds ratio about 3.7 (95% CI 1.5 to 9.1), risk difference 28 percentage points (9 to 48); thought broadcasting 29/69 in schizophrenia vs 8/33, odds ratio about 2.3 (0.9 to 5.7), an unadjusted interval that includes no difference, consistent with the review's statement that this difference was significant only after controlling for age. Woolf intervals for odds ratios, Wald intervals for risk differences; approximate.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable at review level; adjustment in the included studies is listed per study in Table 2 and is mostly limited to matching.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The text summarizes some studies differently from Table 1 (see reporting issues): the visual and tactile hallucination result of McKetin et al. (2017) appears in opposite directions in Table 1 and in the text, and Hajebi et al. (2018) is used in the text but missing from Table 1. Whether relevant studies were left out cannot be checked because excluded records are not listed.
analysis.power: Not assessed. The authors note that small samples may make the two disorders look more alike than they are (Methodological limitations, 3rd paragraph). Four of the twelve Table 1 studies had 15 or fewer people in at least one psychosis group: Medhus et al. (9 methamphetamine-positive), Okada et al. (14 schizophrenia), Tomiyama (11 and 11), Yamamuro et al. (15).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In the direct comparisons, positive-symptom severity was mostly similar in methamphetamine psychosis and schizophrenia; schizophrenia groups had more negative symptoms in every study that examined them in detail (Tomiyama, 1990; Wang et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2015; Hajebi et al., 2018); in the one study that separated acute from persistent cases, the persistent group performed like the schizophrenia group on cognitive tests and the acute group like non-psychotic users and controls (Chen et al., 2015). Acute-sample studies found no methamphetamine–schizophrenia cognitive difference except on one attention test (VSAT) in one study of 30 vs 30. More visual and tactile hallucinations than in schizophrenia were shown directly only in a persistent-psychosis sample (Wang et al., 2016).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says visual and tactile hallucinations appear more prevalent in acute methamphetamine psychosis and that acute methamphetamine psychosis "could be clinically distinguished from a primary psychotic disorder" on behavioural and cognitive features. In the body, the authors themselves say the hallucination-modality differences for acute psychosis come from indirect, not direct, comparisons (Positive symptoms › Acute, 4th paragraph), call the thought-disorder evidence indirect and inconclusive (3rd paragraph), and conclude there is insufficient evidence on whether chronic methamphetamine psychosis is distinct (Summary and conclusions, 2nd paragraph). The parietal-cortex attribution rests on one VSAT difference with no imaging of parietal cortex. Figure 1 orders visual and tactile hallucinations acute > chronic > schizophrenia, which the review's own Table 1 summary of McKetin et al. (2017) contradicts. The management paragraph states as fact that acute symptoms resolve with abstinence, citing a StatPearls chapter rather than the reviewed studies (Summary and conclusions, 3rd paragraph), and the introduction infers methamphetamine-induced persistent changes independent of genetic predisposition from a case report with literature review (Grelotti et al., 2010) (Chronic methamphetamine psychosis paragraph).

timeline.event: McKetin et al. prospective cohort, cited by this review for psychotic symptoms about 5 times more likely during periods of methamphetamine use than during abstinence, with a dose-response relation (Acute methamphetamine psychosis, 3rd paragraph)

Chen et al. (Taiwan): the only included study separating acute (under 1 month) from persistent methamphetamine psychosis with healthy and non-psychotic user controls; persistent group resembled schizophrenia on BPRS positive scores and BACS cognition

McKetin et al. (Australia, 284 people with methamphetamine dependence): no significant difference in lifetime positive symptoms between persistent methamphetamine psychosis and primary psychosis, whose members also used methamphetamine

replication.where_it_stands: At the time of this review the direct-comparison literature was 12–13 mostly small, cross-sectional, hospital-based studies with inconsistent definitions of acute and persistent psychosis, little control of polydrug use or medication, and no pooled estimates.

funding.funder: No research funding statement. Acknowledgments: the first author held an Australian Postgraduate Award and acknowledges a Macquarie University Psychology Department Higher Degree Research Grant.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest. The handling editor (Julia M. Lappin, University of New South Wales) declared a shared affiliation, without other collaboration, with the first author.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychology, Macquarie University, and School of Psychology, University of New South Wales, Sydney, Australia. Article received 28 June 2018, accepted 19 September 2018.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study enrolling people at a first methamphetamine-associated psychotic episode with toxicology-confirmed use, assessed with the same structured, item-level instruments at fixed intervals after verified abstinence, against first-episode schizophrenia patients matched on age, sex, other drug use and antipsychotic exposure, with assessors blind to group; and, for the existing studies, a registered systematic review that pools item-level differences with confidence intervals.

domains.note: Three databases (PubMed, PsycINFO, ScienceDirect), reference lists and Google Scholar were searched with printed terms against inclusion criteria set before the search (Overview of review › Inclusion criteria; Search approach). There are no search dates, record counts or excluded-study list, one author conducted the review (Author contributions), and Hajebi et al. (2018), used in the text and Table 2, is missing from Table 1.

Table 2 records for each of 13 studies the comparison groups, acute/chronic distinction, abstinence and factors controlled, and the text names study limitations, but there is no validated tool. Okada, Yamamuro and Srisurapanont are assigned to acute or chronic psychosis differently across Table 1, Table 2 and the text, and the review's main contrasts depend on that assignment.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Neither author appears in any of the 140 references, including the 13 compared studies (References; Tables 1–2).

The abstract concludes that acute methamphetamine psychosis could be clinically distinguished from schizophrenia by thought disorder, hallucination type and parietal-mediated attention, while the body calls the thought-disorder evidence 'indirect and inconclusive' and the hallucination comparisons not 'reliable' (Positive symptoms › Acute, 3rd–4th paragraphs) and the parietal link rests on one attention test without imaging (Cognitive symptoms › Acute, 2nd paragraph). The management paragraph states that acute symptoms will resolve with abstinence, citing a StatPearls chapter (Summary and conclusions, 3rd paragraph).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for similarity and difference between methamphetamine psychosis and schizophrenia
domains.note: Neither side is under-represented: similar and divergent findings are reported study by study, and the introduction sets out competing explanations (shared vulnerability, methamphetamine-caused schizophrenia, a distinct disorder). The limitations section's arguments on power and total-score scales run only toward differences being missed (Methodological limitations, 3rd paragraph).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High, because the abstract's central conclusion, that acute methamphetamine psychosis can be told apart from schizophrenia, rests on evidence the body itself calls indirect or inconclusive; the search and the appraisal of studies are reported but incomplete. It may be cited as a map of the 12–13 direct-comparison studies and their shared limitations (small, mostly hospital samples; unreported abstinence; uncontrolled polydrug use and medication) and for the point that few studies separate acute from persistent psychosis. It may not be cited for any symptom that distinguishes the two conditions, nor for its introductory prevalence and duration figures.

key_findings.finding: The review identified twelve studies directly comparing methamphetamine psychosis with schizophrenia or primary psychosis, published 1990–2017, with per-study sizes of 22 to 285 as printed; a thirteenth, a 12-month prospective study (Hajebi et al., 2018), is appraised in Table 2 and used in the text but absent from Table 1.
key_findings.locator: Overview of review › Inclusion criteria and Search approach; Table 1; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Positive-symptom severity did not differ between methamphetamine psychosis and schizophrenia in most acute-sample comparisons: PANSS in Medhus et al. (2013; 9 vs 33) and Okada et al. (2016; 21 vs 14), BPRS in Hides et al. (2015; substance-induced vs primary psychotic disorder among 198 people who use methamphetamine), and PANSS at admission, discharge, 6 and 12 months in Hajebi et al. (2018).
key_findings.locator: Positive symptoms › Acute meth psychosis vs. schizophrenia, 2nd paragraph; Table 1 rows 107, 110, 111
key_findings.note: The text attributes a BPRS result to Okada et al. (ref 111), but Table 1 lists PANSS for that study; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Shelly et al. (2016; methamphetamine psychosis within 4 weeks of use n=33, schizophrenia n=69, SCID-I): voices conversing 48.5% vs 20.3%; thought broadcasting 42% in schizophrenia vs 24%, significant only after controlling for age; no difference in other first-rank symptoms.
key_findings.locator: Positive symptoms › Acute meth psychosis vs. schizophrenia, 4th paragraph; Table 1 row 112; Table 2 row 112
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: voices conversing OR about 3.7 (95% CI 1.5–9.1); thought broadcasting OR about 2.3 (0.9–5.7) unadjusted.

key_findings.finding: Srisurapanont et al. (2011; 168 methamphetamine psychosis vs 169 schizophrenia, recent use within the past week, Manchester Scale): Table 1 reports higher methamphetamine-group scores for delusions, hallucinations and incoherent speech, with incoherent speech the only item that differentiated the groups on differential item functioning analysis; negative-symptom severity did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 row 113; Positive symptoms › Acute, 3rd paragraph; Negative symptoms › Acute, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Table 1 prints n=61 for this study against groups of 168 and 169. The text uses this study as evidence that thought disorder marks schizophrenia without giving the direction of the incoherent-speech difference, while Table 1 places the higher score in the methamphetamine group; the direction must be checked in the primary paper.

key_findings.finding: Chen et al. (2015; healthy controls 67, methamphetamine users without psychosis 25, acute psychosis 50, persistent psychosis beyond 1 month of abstinence 56, schizophrenia 54): persistent psychosis equalled schizophrenia on BPRS total and positive scores, both above acute psychosis; negative symptoms schizophrenia > persistent > acute; on BACS, persistent psychosis equalled schizophrenia and both were below acute psychosis and non-psychotic users, which did not differ from controls.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 row 105; Positive symptoms › Chronic, 2nd paragraph; Negative symptoms › Chronic; Cognitive symptoms › Chronic, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The acute group was assessed about 9 weeks after its episode (Table 2), so its lower symptom scores may reflect resolution. Table 1 also says 160 methamphetamine users, but the three user groups sum to 131.

key_findings.finding: Wang et al. (2016; persistent methamphetamine psychosis beyond 1 month of abstinence vs schizophrenia, 53 vs 53 in Table 1): similar delusion patterns and auditory hallucinations; visual and tactile hallucinations more frequent in methamphetamine psychosis; schizophrenia had more negative symptoms overall, with more blunted affect, emotional withdrawal and motor retardation.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 row 115; Positive symptoms › Chronic, 1st paragraph; Negative symptoms › Chronic
key_findings.note: The text gives 52 methamphetamine-psychosis participants and names conceptual disorganization as greater in schizophrenia; Table 1 gives 53 and names unusual thought content.

key_findings.finding: McKetin et al. (2017; 284 people with methamphetamine dependence: 110 without psychosis, 85 transient, 37 persistent beyond 1 month of abstinence, 52 primary psychosis; CIDI lifetime symptoms): no significant difference between persistent methamphetamine psychosis and primary psychosis on any positive symptom; the primary-psychosis group also used methamphetamine.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 row 109; Positive symptoms › Chronic, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Table 1 says the persistent group exceeded the transient group on lifetime visual, olfactory and tactile hallucinations; the text says the persistent and primary groups reported fewer visual and tactile hallucinations than the transient group. The two cannot both be right.

key_findings.finding: Negative symptoms were milder in methamphetamine psychosis than in schizophrenia in the detailed comparisons: Tomiyama (1990; 11 vs 11, SANS) found less affective flattening and alogia but similar avolition–apathy, anhedonia–asociality and attention; Hajebi et al. (2018) found more severe negative symptoms in non-affective psychosis at admission and discharge.
key_findings.locator: Negative symptoms › Acute, 2nd paragraph; Negative symptoms › Chronic; Table 1 row 114

key_findings.finding: Cognition: Jacobs et al. (2008; 19 methamphetamine psychosis vs 20 paranoid schizophrenia) found no difference in any domain; Ezzatpanah et al. (2014; 30 vs 30 vs 30 healthy controls) found both psychosis groups below controls on WCST, Stroop, VSAT and Wechsler Memory Scale, with schizophrenia worse than methamphetamine psychosis only on VSAT; Yamamuro et al. (2015; 15 vs 19) found no BACS differences.
key_findings.locator: Cognitive symptoms › Acute, 1st–2nd paragraphs; Cognitive symptoms › Chronic, 1st paragraph; Table 1 rows 106, 108, 116

key_findings.finding: Prevalence figures cited in the introduction (second-hand, not appraised by the review): 7% to 76% across studies; a 2018 meta-analysis (Lecomte et al.) gave 36.5% for methamphetamine-induced psychotic disorder, 42.7% lifetime and 43.3% among people with methamphetamine use disorder; in an Australian non-treatment sample 13% screened positive for psychosis at assessment and 23% reported clinically significant symptoms in the past year; 60% of a US sample with methamphetamine dependence reported at least one psychotic symptom; risk 2–3 times the general population for recreational use and 11 times for regular use; mean 1.7 years from first use to onset.
key_findings.note: Secondary citations; each must be checked in its primary source before use. The 11-fold figure is cited to a paper whose title concerns crystalline methamphetamine and dependence (ref 41).

key_findings.finding: Duration figures cited (second-hand): most symptoms resolve within 1 month; up to 30% persist up to 6 months after abstinence; 15–28% of admitted patients needed more than 2–3 months in hospital; 10–28% remained psychotic beyond 6 months; 28% had schizophrenia-like symptoms 8–12 years after abstinence (a 1967 Japanese study); a 7% risk of psychotic symptoms during abstinent periods (McKetin et al., 2013); 5% of abstinent people with methamphetamine dependence met criteria for a psychotic disorder at 3-year follow-up.
key_findings.note: Secondary citations from heterogeneous, mostly hospital samples; not appraised by the review.

key_findings.finding: Diagnostic transitions cited (second-hand): 38.8% of Thai patients first hospitalized with methamphetamine psychosis had a schizophrenia diagnosis at 5 years; 5.0% of Chinese patients had their diagnosis changed to schizophrenia; 19.1% to 30% of people admitted with amphetamine-induced psychosis later received a schizophrenia diagnosis in register studies.
key_findings.locator: The relationship between METH-induced psychosis and schizophrenia, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Risk factors cited (second-hand): younger age at first use and larger amounts used, family history of schizophrenia, crystalline methamphetamine, and current use (about 5 times higher odds of psychotic symptoms during periods of use, with a dose-response relation).
key_findings.locator: Acute methamphetamine psychosis, 2nd–3rd paragraphs; The relationship between METH-induced psychosis and schizophrenia, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Indirect comparisons only (different samples, not head-to-head): negative symptoms in 25% and 21.4% of hospitalized methamphetamine-psychosis samples versus 58% (and 50–90% at first episode) in schizophrenia; visual hallucinations in 46.5% and tactile in 21.3% of one methamphetamine-psychosis sample and visual in 68.8% of another, versus 16–27% in schizophrenia. The authors state these hallucination comparisons are not based on direct comparisons.
key_findings.locator: Negative symptoms › Acute, 2nd paragraph; Positive symptoms › Acute, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Studies that did not report abstinence were classed by the authors as acute methamphetamine psychosis; the authors identify mixing of acute and persistent cases, small samples, uncontrolled polydrug use and medication, hospital samples and total-score scales as the main limitations of the literature.
key_findings.locator: Methodological limitations and considerations, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Management remarks are explicitly labelled by the authors as not clinical recommendations: second-generation antipsychotics suggested as possibly appropriate for persistent methamphetamine psychosis, with caution about extrapyramidal effects of first-generation drugs; the authors call for randomized trials.

In its summary, the review cites ref. 140 (Farnia et al., 2014; by its title a randomized trial of aripiprazole versus risperidone for amphetamine-induced psychosis), with ref. 56, for the statement that first-generation antipsychotics such as haloperidol carry an elevated risk of extrapyramidal symptoms in methamphetamine-induced psychosis and should be used carefully; no results of that trial are reported, and the authors label their management remarks as not clinical recommendations.
key_findings.note: Added by the editor during review round 1 so that card and claim agree; the finding was first located by AI reader 2 and has not yet been re-found by a reader who had not seen it.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 summarizes McKetin et al. (2017) as persistent methamphetamine psychosis exceeding transient psychosis on lifetime visual, olfactory and tactile hallucinations; the text says persistent psychosis and primary psychosis reported fewer visual and tactile hallucinations than transient psychosis; Figure 1 orders visual and tactile hallucinations acute > chronic > schizophrenia.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's headline that visual and tactile hallucinations mark acute methamphetamine psychosis depends on which version is right; the primary paper must be read before any claim about hallucination modality by phase.

reporting_issues.issue: The DSM-5 rule is stated two ways: a psychosis persisting longer than 6 months warrants a primary diagnosis (Relationship section, 1st and 3rd paragraphs), but the limitations section says patients psychotic more than 1 month after stopping should, under the DSM, receive a primary diagnosis (Methodological limitations, 2nd paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: The diagnostic threshold that separates substance-induced from primary psychosis must be taken from DSM-5 itself, not from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: Group sizes in Table 1 do not add up: Chen et al. (row 105) lists 160 methamphetamine users but its user groups sum to 131 (25+50+56; 252 total with 67 controls and 54 schizophrenia); Medhus et al. (row 110) prints n=285 against groups of 33 and 9, while Table 2 says 35 of 38 tested positive for methamphetamine and that 13% had taken it recently; Srisurapanont et al. (row 113) prints n=61 against groups of 168 and 169.
reporting_issues.consequence: Sample sizes for these studies must be taken from the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: The same study is described with different instruments: Chen et al. (105) is said to use the PANSS for positive symptoms (Positive symptoms › Chronic, 2nd paragraph) but the BPRS in Table 1 and in the negative-symptom section; Okada et al. (111) is cited for a BPRS result (Positive symptoms › Acute, 2nd paragraph) but listed with the PANSS in Table 1 and in the negative-symptom section.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for conclusions; instruments must be checked at source.

reporting_issues.issue: Acute versus chronic classification is inconsistent: Okada et al. (111) is classed as acute in Table 1 although Table 2 says 15 of its 21 methamphetamine participants had residual and late-onset psychosis; Yamamuro et al. (116) is classed chronic in Table 1, assumed acute in Table 2, and described as acute in the chronic positive-symptom paragraph; Srisurapanont et al. (113) is classed acute in Table 1 while Table 2 says it could include both.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's acute-versus-chronic contrasts, which carry its main conclusions, rest on partly arbitrary assignments.

reporting_issues.issue: Wang et al. (115): 52 methamphetamine-psychosis participants in the text versus 53 in Table 1; conceptual disorganization (text) versus unusual thought content (Table 1) as the item greater in schizophrenia.
reporting_issues.consequence: The thought-disorder conclusion partly rests on this study, so the item matters; check at source.

reporting_issues.issue: The Ezzatpanah et al. VSAT result is called sustained visual attention in the cognitive section and selective visual attention in the abstract and summary.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the parietal-cortex inference in the abstract relies on the selective-attention reading.

reporting_issues.issue: Two secondary citations do not obviously match their claims by title: the 11-fold psychosis risk for regular use cites a paper on crystalline methamphetamine and dependence (ref 41), and the 58% prevalence of negative symptoms in schizophrenia cites a paper on cardiovascular risk and smoking in a schizophrenia cohort (ref 135).
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither figure should be reused without checking the cited source.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 is an image (Venn diagram); only its legend could be read as text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure's content was appraised from the legend only.
